summary: A 1978 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols. It replaced RFC 739 and was replaced by RFC 755. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 750 gathers assigned numbers from several network protocol registries into one reference. It says the list would be updated periodically, and it was later replaced by RFC 755.

questions: how do protocols get numbers assigned
how were network socket numbers assigned
subtitle: A consolidated list of number assignments used by network protocols

tldr.problem: Network protocols used several series of assigned numbers, and developers needed a current list of those values.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compiles link, socket, network, internet message version, protocol number, format and message type assignments in one document.
tldr.outcome: RFC 750 was historic and was later replaced by RFC 755.

today: RFC 750 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 755.

sections.title: A Shared List of Assignments
sections.content:
RFC 750 documents assigned values from several number series used in network protocol implementations. It says the RFC will be updated periodically and that current information can be obtained from Jon Postel, who also handles number assignments.

Developers creating a protocol or application that needs a link, socket or similar number are asked to request an assignment. The RFC points readers to the Protocol Handbook and RFC series for detailed protocol descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: This document brings several number lists together. A developer who needed an assigned number was asked to contact the person managing the assignments.

sections.title: What the Registries Cover
sections.content:
The RFC includes link numbers, socket numbers, network numbers, internet message versions, internet protocol numbers, internet message formats and message types. Each table identifies values that were assigned, reserved or unassigned in this edition.

For example, the socket list divides numbers into network-wide standard functions, host-specific functions, future use and experimental functions. The network-number list describes an 8-bit field used in internetwork protocols then under development; the message-version field is 4 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables cover different number fields used to identify links, services, networks, and protocol details. Each table says which values already had a purpose and which were still open or reserved.

sections.title: Periodic Updates and Status
sections.content:
RFC 750 says the registry will be updated periodically. Its opening identifies it as replacing RFCs 739, 604, 503, 433 and 349; the unit metadata also records RFC 755 as the document that later obsoleted it.

The lists are records of assignments at the time of publication. The RFC directs readers to the cited specifications for details of the protocols that use those numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry was meant to change as assignments changed, so this edition was not permanent. RFC 755 later replaced it.
